hypothesis: An integrated, multi-channel detection stack that combines simple heuristic rules, an off-the-shelf ML signal (e.g., toxicity/semantic anomaly score), and a lightweight human-override workflow will detect emerging AI-driven misinformation narratives earlier (lower detection latency) and with a better balance of precision and coverage than (a) heuristic-only detection or (b) ML-only detection, when applied to the same synthetic event stream.

baseline.name: Heuristics-only Monitoring
baseline.description: A simple rules-based detector that monitors synthetic multi-channel content (simulated social posts, search queries, and owned-channel tickets) and raises alerts when predefined keyword and volume thresholds are crossed. No ML signals or explicit human review; alerts are auto-routed based on static rules.
detection_logic: Keyword match against a small list of configured brand and incident-related terms (e.g., brand name + 'fake', 'leak', 'scandal', 'boycott').
Volume spike detection: rolling count of matching events in a fixed time window (e.g., 10+ hits in 15 minutes on any single channel) triggers an alert.
Channel-agnostic: all channels are treated equally; no weighting or differential thresholds.
baseline.intended_use: Establishes a naive but business-intuitive monitoring approach that many organizations already approximate with basic social listening and manual alert rules. Serves as a reference point for improvements.
implementation_notes: Implemented as a single notebook or script that ingests a timestamped CSV/JSON event stream and applies keyword and volume thresholds.
Configuration kept in a separate plain-text or YAML file to be easily adjustable by non-technical users.

treatment.name: Integrated Heuristics + ML + Human Workflow Detection Stack
treatment.description: A layered detection prototype that ingests the same synthetic multi-channel content but: (1) applies heuristic rules, (2) enriches events with a simple ML-based signal (e.g., toxicity/sentiment/anomaly score from a public model or stubbed local model), and (3) routes suspicious clusters into a basic human triage queue. The system triggers alerts based on combined scores and human confirmations, aiming to surface true emerging misinformation earlier while reducing spurious alerts.
detection_logic: Heuristic layer: same keyword and volume rules as the baseline, but tuned per-channel (e.g., lower thresholds for dark-web-style feed vs. general social).
ML layer: each event receives a score (0–1) representing likelihood of harmful/misleading content (e.g., via a toxicity/sentiment model or stubbed scoring function).
Fusion logic: events are assigned a composite risk score based on weighted combination of heuristics and ML score; emerging clusters are identified via rolling window aggregation.

Human-in-the-loop: events or clusters that exceed a 'review' threshold (lower than the 'auto-alert' threshold) are placed into a simple triage view where a human reviewer (simulated via labels in the synthetic dataset) can confirm or dismiss.

Alerting policy: executive-facing alerts are triggered when (a) composite score exceeds a high threshold OR (b) a human reviewer confirms a cluster as suspicious, even if below the purely numeric threshold.
treatment.intended_use: Demonstrates to executives how combining simple rules, available ML capabilities, and structured human workflows can create a more effective detection layer without building custom deep-learning systems.
implementation_notes: Implemented as a second notebook or script that reuses the same input and configuration formats as the baseline, plus an additional scoring module.
ML scoring can be implemented either via a local, lightweight open-source model or a deterministic stub with configurable scoring heuristics to keep the experiment fully runnable offline.

Human review is simulated using ground-truth labels provided in the synthetic dataset; the notebook demonstrates how different confirmation behaviors (e.g., fast vs. slow reviewers) would affect latency and precision.

workloads.name: WL1_Synthetic_SlowBurn_Deepfake_Rumor
workloads.description: A synthetic event stream simulating a slowly emerging deepfake rumor about a senior executive. The narrative begins in fringe channels (pseudo dark-web forum feed), then leaks into mainstream social and eventually triggers inbound owned-channel queries. This workload tests early-signal detection in low-volume, high-signal environments.

fields: true_narrative_start: boolean (marks first few seeds of the misinformation narrative)

inputs.volume_profile: Gradual increase from ~10 events/hour to ~300 events/hour over 24 simulated hours, with misinfo cluster representing 5–15% of total content.

channel_distribution.phase_2: Social dominates; some search queries begin referencing the rumor.
channel_distribution.phase_3: Owned channels (support tickets, contact forms) receive questions referencing the rumor.

execution_instructions: Run the baseline heuristic-only notebook against wl1_slowburn_deepfake_events.csv, recording all baseline metrics.
Run the integrated stack notebook against the same file, using identical time-window and threshold settings where applicable.
Ensure that both runs are configured to simulate the same executive alert channels (e.g., a 'C-suite alert' flag in outputs) for direct comparability.

workloads.name: WL2_Synthetic_Flash_Boycott_Campaign
workloads.description: A synthetic event stream modeling a rapid, coordinated spike of posts calling for a boycott based on a fabricated product-safety incident. The campaign uses a mix of organic-seeming accounts and bot-like behavior to create a sudden volume spike. This workload stresses the system's ability to handle high volume and discriminate between coordinated misinfo and organic chatter.

inputs.volume_profile: Abrupt spike from ~50 events/hour to >5,000 events/hour within a 2-hour window, decaying back to ~200 events/hour over the next 6 hours.

channel_distribution.initial_spike: Primarily social posts including coordinated hashtags.
channel_distribution.follow_on: Increase in search queries plus inbound owned-channel contacts referencing 'reports' of the fabricated incident.

execution_instructions: Run both baseline and integrated detection notebooks on wl2_flash_boycott_events.csv.
Compare alerting behavior particularly in the early 2-hour spike window.
Optionally, vary thresholds in configuration files to demonstrate sensitivity of both approaches.

workloads.name: WL3_Synthetic_Background_Chatter_With_No_Incident
workloads.description: A synthetic 'day in the life' background dataset with normal brand mentions, customer complaints, marketing-related buzz, and generic news coverage—but no true misinformation incident. This workload evaluates false-positive behavior and alert noise under realistic baseline conditions.

inputs.volume_profile: Stable range of 200–800 events/hour over 24 simulated hours across all channels.

execution_instructions: Run the baseline heuristic-only notebook on wl3_background_chatter_events.csv and record the number and characteristics of alerts.
Run the integrated stack notebook on the same file, using thresholds chosen for WL1 and WL2, without further tuning.
Evaluate the rate and nature of false alerts (alerts with no corresponding ground-truth misinfo).

shared_configuration: Use the same input datasets (identical files) for baseline and treatment for each workload.
Use a consistent time-window size for volume aggregation (e.g., 15-minute windows) across both conditions.
Keep keyword lists, brand terms, and initial thresholds identical at the start of each comparison run; any tuning should be documented and applied symmetrically where possible.
Run both baseline and integrated prototypes in the same runtime environment (Python version, library versions) to avoid performance or compatibility confounders.
randomness_and_seeding: If the ML scoring component uses any stochastic behavior (e.g., probabilistic sampling), fix a random seed and record it in configuration.
All simulations of human-review timing should use deterministic durations for the primary experiment; any stochastic human-behavior simulations should be clearly demarcated as exploratory.
observer_blindness: When feasible, reviewers evaluating the outputs (e.g., alert logs) should not be informed whether a given run is baseline or treatment when assessing business usefulness of alerts.
Output files should be anonymized as 'Run A' and 'Run B' per workload for subjective assessments.
execution_order: To avoid order effects, alternate whether the baseline or treatment is run first for a given workload when multiple teams or sessions are conducted.
For a single-user run-through, document the order of execution; for reproducibility, scripts should default to baseline-first but allow override.

metrics.name: time_to_first_true_alert_minutes
metrics.description: Elapsed simulated time between the first ground-truth misinformation event (true_narrative_start == true or first is_ground_truth_misinfo == true) and the first alert that correctly corresponds to that misinfo cluster.

metrics.name: time_to_reliable_detection_minutes
metrics.description: Elapsed simulated time between the first ground-truth misinfo event and the point where cumulative precision for alerts on that cluster exceeds a configurable threshold (e.g., 0.7), indicating reliable detection rather than a one-off lucky alert.

metrics.name: alert_precision
metrics.description: Number of alerts that correspond to true misinformation clusters divided by total alerts generated over the evaluation window.

metrics.name: alert_recall_cluster_level
metrics.description: Number of distinct ground-truth misinformation clusters that generated at least one alert divided by total number of ground-truth clusters in the workload.

metrics.name: executive_alert_volume_per_24h
metrics.description: Total number of alerts that meet the criteria for C-suite/executive routing within a 24-hour simulated period.

metrics.name: reviewer_load_events_per_reviewer_hour
metrics.description: Number of events or clusters routed to human reviewers divided by total (simulated) reviewer hours in the scenario, indicating operational workload for human intelligence.

metrics.name: estimated_detection_cost_index
metrics.description: A composite index approximating detection cost, based on a weighted combination of computational complexity (e.g., events processed x relative compute weight), number of human review actions, and alert volume routed to high-attention channels. Designed to be comparable across baseline and treatment as a directional cost metric rather than a monetary value.

metrics.name: coverage_by_channel
metrics.description: For each channel (social, search, dark_web, owned), the ratio of ground-truth misinformation events that are associated with at least one detected alert.

metrics.name: mean_false_alerts_per_24h
metrics.description: Average number of alerts over a 24-hour window that do not correspond to any ground-truth misinformation cluster (i.e., pure noise).

metrics.name: latency_distribution_percentiles
metrics.description: Key percentiles (e.g., 25th, 50th, 75th) of the distribution of times between ground-truth misinformation event occurrence and first related alert, computed per cluster and then aggregated.

primary: For WL1_Synthetic_SlowBurn_Deepfake_Rumor, the integrated treatment reduces time_to_first_true_alert_minutes by at least 20% compared to baseline, without more than a 25% increase in mean_false_alerts_per_24h.

For WL2_Synthetic_Flash_Boycott_Campaign, the integrated treatment achieves equal or better alert_precision (within ±0.05 absolute) compared to baseline while reducing executive_alert_volume_per_24h by at least 20%, indicating better prioritization.
Across WL1 and WL2 combined, the integrated treatment improves alert_recall_cluster_level by at least 10 percentage points relative to baseline.
secondary: For WL3_Synthetic_Background_Chatter_With_No_Incident, the integrated treatment produces fewer or equal executive_alert_volume_per_24h and mean_false_alerts_per_24h than the baseline, demonstrating that added sophistication does not make background noise worse.

The estimated_detection_cost_index for the integrated treatment remains within 1.5x of the baseline cost index for each workload, providing an acceptable trade-off between improved detection and operational cost.

coverage_by_channel for dark_web and owned channels improves under the integrated treatment by at least 10 percentage points relative to baseline in WL1 and WL2, highlighting better visibility in non-obvious channels.
interpretation_for_executives: If the integrated stack shows earlier and more reliable detection with manageable alert and reviewer loads, it suggests that executives should prioritize layered detection investments (rules + ML + human workflows) rather than relying solely on keyword/volume monitoring.

If improvements are marginal or costs appear disproportionate, executives can use the metrics to scope smaller, targeted enhancements (e.g., adding human review only for high-risk channels) before committing to full-stack changes.

failure_modes.name: Overfitting_Thresholds_To_Synthetic_Data
failure_modes.description: Tuning thresholds aggressively on the provided synthetic workloads may yield unrealistically strong performance that does not generalize to real-world data, giving executives a false sense of confidence.
mitigations: Provide default threshold configurations with minimal tuning and clearly label any hyper-optimized settings as 'demo only'.
Encourage users to apply the same configuration to multiple, distinct synthetic workloads (WL1–WL3) and note performance variability.

failure_modes.name: Misinterpreting_Synthetic_Timelines_As_Real_Time
failure_modes.description: Readers might confuse simulated time with actual wall-clock time and draw incorrect conclusions about how quickly real-world detection would occur.
mitigations: Clearly annotate in notebooks that timestamps are simulated and explain how to scale the interpretation (e.g., what a 30-minute simulated latency might mean in practice).
Include commentary on operational constraints (API rate limits, human staffing) that can increase real-world latency.

failure_modes.name: Unstable_ML_Scoring_Due_To_External_APIs
failure_modes.description: If ML scoring relies on external APIs, rate limits, network issues, or model changes could alter results over time or make the experiments non-reproducible.
mitigations: Default to a local, deterministic scoring stub for the core experiment, optionally providing external API integrations as clearly marked extensions.
Version-control both local models and scoring logic; record model/version identifiers in experiment metadata.

failure_modes.name: Human_Review_Simulation_Not_Reflecting_Reality
failure_modes.description: Simulated human reviewer behavior (e.g., immediate decisions, perfect labeling) may not reflect real-world delays, errors, and disagreements, biasing latency and precision results in favor of human-in-the-loop designs.
mitigations: Provide adjustable parameters for reviewer delay and error rates; encourage users to explore more realistic settings.
Document that base runs use 'idealized' human performance and include separate scenarios with more conservative assumptions.

failure_modes.name: Metric_Misinterpretation_By_Non_Technical_Users
failure_modes.description: Executives may misinterpret metrics like precision/recall or cost indices, leading to incorrect decisions (e.g., over-valuing coverage at the expense of unmanageable alert volumes).
mitigations: Include a brief, executive-readable glossary in the repository explaining each metric and common tradeoffs.
Provide pre-built dashboard cells or views that relate metrics back to business concepts (e.g., 'alerts per executive per day').

failure_modes.name: Dataset_Leakage_Between_Configuration_And_Evaluation
failure_modes.description: Using workload-specific knowledge (e.g., knowing exactly which keywords appear in misinfo content) to design rules may result in unrealistically high performance.
mitigations: Offer a default keyword list that is not perfectly aligned with each misinfo narrative, reflecting real-world uncertainty.
Encourage users to define configuration before inspecting ground-truth labels; document when and how any post-hoc tuning is done.

recommended_libraries: scikit-learn >= 1.3.0 (for simple ML scoring or evaluation utilities)
optional_libraries: textblob or similar (for basic sentiment analysis, if desired)
fastapi or flask (only if building a live alerting prototype API, not required for core experiments)
hardware_requirements: Any modern laptop or cloud instance with at least 4 GB RAM.
No GPU is required; all ML can be run on CPU with small models or stub scoring.
setup_instructions: Create and activate a virtual environment (e.g., python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate on Unix/macOS or .venv\\Scripts\\activate on Windows).
Install dependencies: pip install -r requirements.txt (or run a provided setup script).
Launch Jupyter: jupyter lab or jupyter notebook, then open the chapter 3 notebooks under notebooks/.

run_instructions: Step 1: Environment Preparation
1.1 Follow the setup_instructions under required_environment to install dependencies and launch Jupyter.
1.2 Verify that the data/ directory contains wl1_slowburn_deepfake_events.csv, wl2_flash_boycott_events.csv, and wl3_background_chatter_events.csv.
Step 2: Configure Detection Parameters
2.1 Open config/ch03_detection_config.yaml and review default settings, including:
- keyword_list: list of brand and incident terms.
- volume_thresholds: counts per 15-minute window per channel.
- ml_score_thresholds: thresholds for 'review' vs. 'auto-alert'.
- human_review_delay_minutes: simulated human response time.
2.2 For the main experiment, keep defaults unchanged to allow reproducible comparison with documented results.
Step 3: Run Baseline (Heuristics-Only) for Each Workload
3.1 Open notebooks/ch03_baseline_heuristics.ipynb.
3.2 In the notebook, set the workload parameter to 'WL1' and input path to data/wl1_slowburn_deepfake_events.csv.
3.3 Execute the notebook cells sequentially to:
- Load the dataset.
- Apply heuristic rules to generate alerts.
- Compute metrics defined in the metrics section.
- Save results to outputs/baseline_wl1_results.json (or similar).
3.4 Repeat steps 3.2–3.3 for 'WL2' (data/wl2_flash_boycott_events.csv) and 'WL3' (data/wl3_background_chatter_events.csv), saving outputs to separate files.
Step 4: Run Treatment (Integrated Stack) for Each Workload
4.1 Open notebooks/ch03_integrated_stack.ipynb.
4.2 Ensure that it is referencing the same config/ch03_detection_config.yaml file.
4.3 Set the workload parameter to 'WL1' and input path to data/wl1_slowburn_deepfake_events.csv.
4.4 Execute the notebook cells sequentially to:
- Load the dataset.
- Apply heuristic rules plus ML scoring to compute composite risk scores.
- Simulate routing of selected events/clusters to human review and update decisions.
- Generate alerts based on combined logic.
- Compute metrics and save to outputs/integrated_wl1_results.json.
4.5 Repeat for 'WL2' and 'WL3', saving outputs to integrated_wl2_results.json and integrated_wl3_results.json respectively.
Step 5: Compare Baseline and Treatment
5.1 Use a comparison cell or a separate notebook (e.g., notebooks/ch03_compare_results.ipynb) to load pairs of results files (baseline vs. integrated) per workload.
5.2 For each workload, compute deltas for:
- time_to_first_true_alert_minutes
- time_to_reliable_detection_minutes
- alert_precision
- alert_recall_cluster_level
- executive_alert_volume_per_24h
- mean_false_alerts_per_24h
- estimated_detection_cost_index
5.3 Visualize results via bar charts or tables that clearly label baseline vs. integrated performance.
5.4 Optionally, generate simple executive-ready views (e.g., 'Under the integrated stack, you would have seen this rumor X minutes earlier with Y fewer/noise alerts.').
Step 6: Sensitivity and Scenario Exploration (Optional)
6.1 Adjust thresholds and keyword lists in config/ch03_detection_config.yaml to simulate different risk appetites (e.g., more sensitive vs. more conservative detection).
6.2 Re-run selected workloads under both baseline and integrated conditions with the new configuration, saving results with versioned filenames.
6.3 Document how changes affect metrics such as precision, recall, and executive alert volume; use these insights as discussion prompts for leadership tradeoffs.
Step 7: Document Findings
7.1 Populate a simple template (e.g., docs/ch03_executive_summary_template.md) with:
- Key metric comparisons per workload.
- Observed tradeoffs between coverage, latency, precision, and cost.
- Implications for your organization's preferred detection stack design (build, buy, or partner).
7.2 Save this summary for use in executive team or board briefings.

fields: run_id: string (unique identifier per execution, e.g., UUID)
code_version: string (git commit hash or tag)
config_version: string (hash or filename of YAML configuration)
coverage_by_channel: object (keys: channel names; values: float ratios)
timestamp: ISO-8601 string (simulated event time at which alert fired)
interpretive_notes: string|null (brief narrative on tradeoffs observed)
